title: Handle lead-acid batteries safely
summary: Move, connect, charge and store lead-acid batteries without acid burns, short-circuit burns, hydrogen explosions or back injuries. Covers car, golf cart, forklift, floor scrubber, UPS and solar batteries.

materials.item: Distilled water, or clean rainwater caught straight into a clean plastic container, for topping up flooded batteries

steps.text: Put on glasses and gloves. Check the battery before you touch it: cracks, bulges, leaks, white crust, a wet top.
steps.warn: A cracked or bulging battery can pour acid when tipped. Keep it upright.

steps.text: Wrap the handle of your wrench in tape, leaving only the jaws bare.
steps.warn: A wrench across the terminals of a big battery can weld itself on, glow red and burst the battery.

steps.text: On a vehicle or machine, switch everything off. Undo the negative (−, black) lead first, then the positive (+, red). When reconnecting, positive first and negative last.
steps.warn: If you undo the positive while the negative is still on, a wrench touching the frame makes a dead short.

steps.text: Lift with both hands by the handles or a strap, knees bent, battery close to your body. Car batteries weigh about 15–25 kg, golf cart batteries about 30 kg. Forklift batteries weigh hundreds of kilograms or more and need machinery.
steps.warn: Don't hug a battery to your chest or let it tilt. Acid can slop out of the vents.

steps.text: Carry it upright, strapped down, with the terminals covered by a cap, a rag or tape, away from metal tools.
Charge in a ventilated place, away from sleeping areas, sparks and flames. Connect the charger to the battery before switching the charger on. Switch off before unclipping.
steps.warn: Charging makes hydrogen. A spark at the terminals can blow the top off the battery.

steps.text: On flooded batteries with removable caps, check the level after charging. Top up with distilled water to the fill mark, or to just cover the plates. Never add acid.
steps.warn: Don't overfill. Acid will bubble out during the next charge.

steps.text: Clean crust off terminals with a paste of baking soda and water and a brush, then rinse with clean water. Keep the paste out of the cells.
Store batteries fully charged in a cool place, and top up the charge every month or two.
steps.warn: A flat battery can freeze and crack a few degrees below zero. A fully charged one survives hard frost.

steps.text: Neutralise any spill with baking soda until it stops fizzing, soak it up with dirt or sawdust, and rinse. Keep dead batteries upright on a tray outdoors, away from water sources.

notes:
## What's inside

A 12 V lead-acid battery is six cells of about 2.1 V each, so about 12.6–12.7 V when full. Lead plates sit in dilute sulphuric acid.

| Type | How to tell | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Flooded (wet) | Removable caps on top | Can be topped up with distilled water. Must stay upright |
| AGM | Sealed, often marked AGM | Acid held in glass mat. Don't open. Tolerates tipping better |
| Gel | Sealed, marked gel | Needs a slightly lower charge voltage. Don't open |

Most 12 V batteries charge at roughly 14.4 V and float at about 13.5 V. Gel types use a little less. Check the label if there is one.

## Short circuits

A car battery can push hundreds of amps through a short. That is enough to melt a wrench, a ring or a watch strap in seconds. A ring shorted across a terminal can burn a finger to the bone. Take jewellery off.

## Hydrogen

Hydrogen burns or explodes when it makes up about 4% or more of the air. It collects in the cells and under the lid during and just after charging. That is why the last jump-start clamp goes on bare engine metal away from the battery, not on the battery's negative post.

## Freezing

| State of charge | Roughly freezes at |
|---|---|
| Full | well below −40 °C |
| Half | about −20 to −25 °C |
| Flat | not far below 0 °C, about −10 °C or warmer |

Never charge a frozen battery. Let it thaw first, and check for cracks.

## Common mistakes

- Charging a frozen or bulging battery.
- Topping up with tap water or salty water instead of distilled water.
- Leaving a battery flat after use. It sulphates and loses capacity fast.
- Wearing a ring or watch while working on terminals.
- Mixing old and new batteries in one bank.
